title: Home
text:
This EF2023 Dashboard is a grouping and visual summary of Canada Energy Regulator’s raw data on future outlooks for Canadian energy. Its purpose is to highlight the projected importance of energy sources across Canada as it adheres to net-zero targets up to 2050.
To focus on energy sources, this rendition tabulates drivers affecting projected importance under demand, availability, trade and emissions1.
Takeaway examples, summary statistics, and data dictionaries are provided with every main tab within hoverable sidebars2 or definition boxes.

text:
Demand


Domestic primary demand decreasing partly4.

Net-zero demand driven down by Natural Gas plus Refined Petroleum Products5
Demand driven up by Landfill Gas and Other Renewables plus Nuclear energy6




Domestic secondary demand decreasing7.

Demand driven down mainly by Natural Gas8, esp. in Industry.
Demand driven up mainly by Electricity, plus Hydrogen9, esp. in Transportation.

title: Home
text:
Availability

Domestic Natural Gas and Crude Oil production decreasing10.

Production projected to peak in 2030 or 2026 before decreasing11.

Domestic Electricity and Hydrogen production increasing12.
High hydrogen production growth13.

title: Home
text:
Trade

Hydrocarbon supply and demand in equilibrium barring Ethane:

Domestic Ethane demand projected constant in all scenarios14.
Ethane production projected decreasing, requiring imports in Net-zero scenarios15.

Global Net-zero Pentanes+ production surplus making it a potential new future export (past 2040).

title: Home
text:
Emissions

~75% emission cuts between 2022 and 2050 may enable carbon offsets sufficient for Net-zero.

Simultaneous reduction and absorption is needed (target at ~165 to 155 MtCO2eq/yr).
Top 3 carbon-intensive sectors are Oil and Gas, Transportation, and Buildings (over 60%)16.
Top 3 carbon removal pathways involve LULUCF, DAC, and Electricity.
Electricity may be carbon-neutral by 2035 (both Net-zero scenarios).


The About section contains information on the dataset source and further project details.

title: About
text: The dashboard and accompanying pages were built in R using Quarto and an R package developed for this purpose. Data source details, the dashboard hierarchy, and a data dictionary are each provided below.

title: About
text:
Footnotes


Bar stacking currently relies on Plotly’s default JS y axis rescaling behavior. This fallback is used because a single custom function is used to generate all views (adding traces by graphing mode). This implies that y limits adjust more reliably from frame to frame (i.e., scenarios) on redrawing events (e.g., when views are reset or a legend item is (de)selected).↩︎
Exceptionally, some (like Hydrogen production) start in 2010, and projections-only trends start in 2023).↩︎
Exceptions are made for Scenarios (always listed as: Current Measures, Canada Net-zero, Global Net-zero) and plots with multiple nested levels (sorted alphabetially as a fallback).↩︎
Segments sliding along y axes on plots with line-type traces.↩︎
Complementary (dictionary information not specified).↩︎
Complementary (dictionary information not specified).↩︎
This reflects the following logical progression by design: The relevance of future energy sources (i.e., the dashboard’s main theme) starts with Demand. It must therefore be covered by Supply, which motivates Trade streams as per pricing dynamics. This results in Emissions, which is monitored across sectors. This exact progression is reflected across tabs to make this layout easier to digest.↩︎
Within the R ecosystem, Plotly was selected for its high customizablility, even through e.g., R’s highcharter wrapper functions handle narrow viewport visuals and swipe gestures better (based on visual similarity alone, highchart is likely the graph framework used by CER).↩︎
Two plotly buttons cannot share the "animate" method at the same time. Therefore, slicers use "update" instead.↩︎
R package shareable by request.↩︎
